title: When Help Isn't Helpful
subtitle: A prayer for a new mother answered still didn't make my sister's abandonment go away.
body_html:
As a child psychiatrist, when I was in my 30s, I learned about the strange world of the adopted. Most people—or, at least, your author—imagine adoption to be a positive thing. A family chooses to take in a child. In my mind, adopted children were all orphaned in a freak accident, and there is no one to blame. It barely registered with me that my own family included an adopted daughter. Alison Muir, my older sister, was always just my sister. I knew she was a half-sister, only the biological input from my dad. But she had a mom—Vita—who was also my mom. She was my sister, and that was it.

She was that, and our mother loved her. The difference, of course, is that another mother chose not to love her before she had a mother choose her.

I’ve written about this topic before, in this prior article, and in this one as well.

Both Vita and Alison have prominent roles in my poetry collection, “The Hellthread.” (Amazon affiliate link).

And yes, I’m obviously working on a few books in the background (three to be exact).

VITA: She had written a note and put it under her pillow.

OWEN: Like for the Tooth Fairy.

VITA: Asking God to send her a mother. Enter me. This was a mother who locked her children out of the house so she could have her own quiet and privacy. And so there I was.

OWEN: Which was home?

VITA: Yeah. She locked her kids out of the house that she was in. She didn’t want to be bothered with them between three and five. So she said, go out and play. And this was in some part of New Jersey. Very nice suburb. They were safe, but.

OWEN: What was the town?

VITA: Woodcliff Lake.

OWEN: Woodcliff Lake. Okay. So to get her own quiet time, she just locked her children out of her home.

VITA: Yes. I don’t even know her name, by the way.

OWEN: Elizabeth.

VITA: Elizabeth.

OWEN: Okay.

VITA: So Elizabeth was Betty in her early life, and thinking it was chic, Liz in her later life.

OWEN: Oh, so she changed it from...

VITA: Betty Bonfonte.

OWEN: Betty Bonfonte...

VITA: ...to Liz Bonfonte. What, Liz Muir?

OWEN: Liz Muir, right, when she married Art. Okay, so Alison was the daughter of Art Muir and Betty Bonfonte.

VITA: Nay, Liz Muir. No, nay. Oh, no, no, no. Nay is the... Betty Bonfonte, nay Liz Muir.

OWEN: No, wait. Betty Bonfonte?

VITA: Yes. You had it backwards. Liz Muir, nay Betty Bonfonte.

OWEN: The sequencing matters.

VITA: And so Alison was praying for a mother and then you met her dad.

OWEN: Can you walk me into the house when you first met Alison? Just verbally walk me through what you saw, what you smelled, et cetera.

VITA: Oh. So I walked in the front door and your dad showed me around. I have one word to describe it. Ecru.

OWEN: What is ecru?

VITA: Ecru is a color that’s completely noncommittal. It’s a kind of off-white. Beige-ish. She had hired a decorator. The decorator, apparently, didn’t either. And the house was very sparse. He invited me into the living room and gestured toward a chair. So I sat in the chair, and he said, “Oh, great. Now it’s down to five hundred dollars a sit.” And the whole household went like that.

But at that time, Alison had a room that was like a monk’s cell, which was next to her sister’s room, the preferred child by the mother, which looked like a bad version of a French provincial world. Alison didn’t have a rug, she had shades instead of drapes, she didn’t have anything.

Anyway, so I show up in this ecru world, and I come to make dinner for them. And Alison, unbeknownst to me, had on afternoons when she was alone in the house been watching little cooking shows and writing down recipes. So I’m making something, and she’s tiny and skinny, and she jumps up on the counter.

She was very pretty, photogenic, sort of exotic looking. She had this notion of wanting to be a model. She wasn’t tall enough, and she wasn’t quite pretty enough. So she swung from being very vain to being very insecure, and it really wasn’t ever a healthy middle ground.

She stares at what I’m doing. I’m breading something, and she’s sticking her hands into the breadcrumbs and tasting it. And that was the beginning of our relationship. That was the icebreaker.

And when I ultimately lived with her, I did things like sign her up for cooking classes. There was a lady in town who did cooking classes, so she signed up for Thai food, making dumplings, whatever it was.

OWEN: Can you speak about the relationship between Alison and me when I was a kid?

VITA: Oh, she loved you. She absolutely loved you. She had gotten married, but a ridiculous marriage.

OWEN: George?

VITA: No, not George. That was [her sister] Karen’s boyfriend. I don’t even remember this one’s name. He was also a chef, who thought that he’d married into a rich family and basically stopped working the day he married her.

[A bird appears at the window.]

VITA: Oh, look at that beautiful bird. It’s a robin. No, it’s a cardinal.

OWEN: Yes.

[the bird flies away]

VITA: You were maybe two at the time, and you said that you wanted orange juice. But you wanted the orange juice with juicy bits. And she used to love to tease you about the juicy bits. She loved having you around.

OWEN: She called me Brub.

VITA: So I remember you, as a very young child, getting your genitalia trapped in the zipper of footy pajamas, which was a hard...

OWEN: I was hoping you’d tell that story.

VITA: And screaming. And forever onward, that would be known as Brub’s Peep. I think you missed the memo about wearing the footy pajamas with underpants so you don’t get your peep trapped in the zipper. But Brub’s Peep. That was Alison’s whole thing.

Her sense of humor was ridiculous. She had a million names for people, and they would evolve. I have no idea how her sister Karen went from Ka to Imbrebin. But there was always this evolution of nicknames. Lindsey went from Binz to Binzel, then Binzelbop, Linzer Tort, Lindzer Bean, and then just Bean. So Alison was the font of all nicknames.

OWEN: Most kids who love cooking don’t go to La Varenne.

VITA: Well, she got more and more deeply involved in it. And she didn’t want to go to college. She didn’t want to go to the Culinary Institute of America. Which is ironic, because she ended up teaching there and being their youngest Chef de Cuisine ever—and the only woman.

OWEN: Can you tell the difference between a chef de cuisine and anything else? What were women traditionally doing?

VITA: Pastry chefs. They were all pastry chefs. Yeah, there’s sexism in cooking. It’s not a liberal society. It’s a male-dominated society.

OWEN: Ironic, if you’re not French, I guess.

VITA: Yes, it’s really. But chef de cuisine, that’s the person who plans the meal. And tells the pastry chef what desserts to make.

OWEN: And she went to La Varenne to become the first woman to become a chef de cuisine.

VITA: Not to do that, but that was the endgame. It was a long road to that. La Varenne is a fancy cooking school. It was where the wives of rich men went to learn how to cook as a hobby. But it was a serious cooking school. She really learned it, it was very authentic French cooking, from the ground up.

OWEN: It had nothing to do with the Frenchness. It had everything to do with the food. France has a couple of institutions. I think of the Sorbonne.

VITA: As what? That’s a university.

OWEN: Well, sure, but they have the institution for the thing. They are not like the U.S. with the embarrassment of riches around higher education. They’ve got one and you go to the one.

VITA: And French cooking is the cooking for the world, right? That’s the most developed cuisine.

OWEN: I think so too. There isn’t a lot of room for improvisation. In standard, dyed-in-the-wool French cuisine, they’re a rule.

VITA: Well, it’s a textual religion. It’s pretty obsessive. She would say things like, I can’t follow rules. I read cookbooks for ideas and then I go cook. Julia Child told you that you put the thing in the middle third of the oven and you cooked it for seven and a half minutes.

OWEN: This wasn’t a peasant cuisine.

VITA: No, this is for the high class.

OWEN: And when she came back and started her working life, what was that like?

VITA: Well, I sat her down. I can remember sitting at your father’s desk up in the Eyrie. Where can you take this? You could work in a restaurant. You could teach. She said, well, how would I do that? And so I said, maybe you could intern somewhere, and see if you could get some sort of credential from doing that. And there was a school that had started in Farmington, which wasn’t far from us. So she went there to work.

Then having had that background, she went to work in various restaurants in the area. And there was always one disaster after another, because restaurants are full of people who are overworked, underpaid, and exhausted. So there’s a high incidence of substance abuse in restaurants. She worked in a chic little bistro in New Milford. But the owner was a dreadful alcoholic, and by the time the evening was over, he was really in his cups, so she got stuck doing everything. And he had this industrial-sized box of Saran Wrap. So she’s cleaning up things and wrapping things, and it’s not in a holder, which it should have been. She pulls it down accidentally on herself, and that blade cut her wrist so that she had to have immediate restorative surgery for this dreadful injury.

And she also had a congenital malformation of the end of her back. Coincidentally, I have the same thing. It’s called spondylolisthesis, and it’s not contagious. We were both born with it. And you don’t want to overstress that sacral area. And she was doing it all the time, because they would send her, the sous chef, or the assistant to the sous chef, down to the basement to bring up a bushel of potatoes.

She ended up at the French Culinary Institute in Manhattan.

I have a picture of her in her chef’s attire. She looks suntanned in that picture. And her hair is drawn back, because you’ve got to have your hair out of the way. She clipped it back with an elastic. She had a wonderful head of really curly, unruly hair that now people love, but then she was always trying to straighten. And the chef’s uniform is wonderful. It was a sort of Mandarin collar that you buttoned to the side, and then she had an apron that came around and tied in the front. Pure white. All pure white. She had trouble with her feet, so she wore those clogs.

They had a restaurant they called L’Ecole, where their students would train and work, and it served the public.

OWEN: Training ground.

VITA: I had vichyssoise, the potato leek soup. It was the first time I ever had a chilled soup, and I’ve loved chilled soup to this day. So she taught the students there, and they loved her, because she was very authentic and very funny and very dedicated. At the end of every school session they would give her presents, like a Cuisinart. And I’ll never forget her doing a class there. She’s facing the audience, and she’s got a little cooking station, and she’s making something with shrimp, and she’s showing you that you use the shells of the shrimp. You don’t waste anything. You boil that up and you get an essence of shrimp. She said, “Remember, never waste perfectly good shrimp shells.”

So she did all right there, but I think she had started using something when she was there.

OWEN: It would make sense that she was exposed to enough substances.

VITA: And she started to become paranoid. So-and-so was taking her food out of the refrigerator, or putting stuff in the refrigerator that would get her in trouble.

OWEN: Some of this is true, because I’ve heard these stories from other people. There is backstabbing in the kitchen.

VITA: Right. Highly patriarchal. So she decided she would get out of that and go to something else. She had gotten divorced from this first husband already.

OWEN: Useless man.

VITA: So she looked for another job, and she saw a job for a person who lived in Columbus, Ohio. And it turned out to be the person. There’s only one person who matters who lives in Columbus, Ohio. Leslie Wexner. And we didn’t know anything about Leslie Wexner at the time. It turned out that he owned Victoria’s Secret. And she was hired to be the chef for the family and all the visitors who would come in their airplanes.

OWEN: Jeffrey Epstein.

VITA: Yes. Like, literally, she was cooking for Jeffrey. She said that this man’s estate had twenty-seven kitchens. And she’s expected to cook for everybody. The guests would come, and they would come with the wife and the kids, and the nannies for the kids, and she was expected to cook for everybody. And she didn’t even have help in the kitchen or anyone to clean up. And finally, her back really gave out, and his physician said, " That girl has to go to bed, and she’s got to stay there for nine weeks.” They had her up in, I don’t know, a week.

So she applied for a job at the Culinary Institute of America.

OWEN: And she did get it.

VITA: She did get it. And the job was Chef de Cuisine. So your sister Lindsay went to Columbus and stayed with her, helping her through the recovery period after the surgery.

So she goes to a doctor, she finds a Doctor Feelgood, who slaps morphine patches on her arms. She figured out how to accelerate the delivery of morphine. You put a hairdryer on it, and you make it come faster, or you put two of them on, and it’s even better.

OWEN: These were fentanyl patches.

VITA: Yes. And none of us knew what fentanyl was.

OWEN: What year was this?

VITA: We lived in Washington, Connecticut at the time.

OWEN: 1987. Well, before the opioid epidemic was a thing, anyone knew about. These were still drugs that treated pain.

VITA: So she disappeared off the face of the planet at one point, and your father and I went to find her, to see her apartment in disarray. We finally found her and took her to a hospital. The hospital said no, we don’t treat this sort of thing. Then we went through three hospitals in one night. The last one said, well, this has been legally prescribed to her. She’s an adult. This hospital doesn’t want to have anything to do with it. So they won’t admit her.

And you and I know from experience now that had they admitted her, it would have been a seventy-two hour hold anyway. So your father and I put her in the car. We figured we’d take her home, because nobody had eaten all day. She’s in the back, and she starts talking to us. She says, what did you guys do all day?

And the next day she was literally out of her mind. She was searching madly on the floor in her room, in her purse. She was looking for drugs that might have fallen in the bottom of the purse. So I called the doctor she had been seeing in Tivoli. And he said, you want to be very careful. She could be dangerous. And get her to a hospital as soon as you can.

OWEN: Which you had done the day before.

VITA: So I took her to the hospital. Your father was probably gone, because he was gone five or six days a week. So this was all me. All me, all the time.

OWEN: With your adopted child.

VITA: Yes. And so I take her to the hospital, and we leave her there. But they don’t put her in the psychiatric ward. They put her in the medical ward. I go the next morning and I walk into the bathroom, and there’s no sink in the bathroom. And I go to the nursing station and I said, are you aware of the fact that there’s no sink in that bathroom? They said yes. I said, and? They said she ripped it out of the wall.

Then they put her in the psychiatric ward. And they were so bad, and she was so manipulative, that she got them to give her, I forget what drug it was...

OWEN: Vicodin.

VITA: Yeah, one of those drugs. Completely contraindicated. Twenty years of her leading this failed life, me trying to save what was left of it.

Her first suicide attempt, was that when she slashed her wrist?

OWEN: No, there was a throat one. Was that not the first?

VITA: There was a wrist, but there was a throat. I remember the scar very clearly. There were some attempts I’m blocking out.

OWEN: She was evaluated in an ER for slashing her throat. She then, a week later, was admitted after the acetaminophen overdose that led to liver toxicity.

VITA: Right. And so on that one, she was then living in New Jersey, because I think she got a job there, a teaching job. So I go to the hospital, and they tell me that she’s got liver failure.

OWEN: I believe what you told me on the phone was, “We don’t waste good livers on suicides.”

VITA: So that’s what they said. And miraculously she recovered. And from that day on, she was mine. I brought her home to live with us. I took her to meetings at the hospital. We tried to support her and get her an apartment, to see if she could manage on her own. And this went on and on and on and on.

And it was hopeless. It was absolutely hopeless. She got a job in Philadelphia, and she was involved in some sort of fire. We never got the details of this. She said something caught on fire on the stove.

OWEN: I heard the report from the doctor. There was a shoe on the stove.

VITA: She left her shoe on the stove. But at the same time, there was an injury to her leg that she said came from someone who broke into the apartment. She might have been conflating two stories.

So she was in the hospital for some time, and then they sent her to a nursing home to recover further from this ghastly leg wound.

OWEN: I remember. That was when I was in residency. I talked to the doctor briefly, and he said she had a mini-mental status exam score of thirteen, which is in the demented range. I guess it was delirium at the time, but they didn’t seem to understand that.

VITA: Anyway, so then we rescued her from that. I couldn’t make the trip. So dear Albert Rivera did it for me. He went and picked her up with all her stuff and brought her home. And so she was living at home, driving your father, who was ill, absolutely nuts, because she had logorrhea. He’d sit down and try to relax and watch a program on television, and she wouldn’t stop talking. And this was after his first stroke in France. That was a left MCA stroke, so his receptive language was impaired. And I’m dealing with both of them simultaneously, and a full-time challenging job. That was a circus.

She got on Social Security disability, which she really needed to be on. She was legitimately disabled. And I found her an apartment. It was the worst decision of my life. I found an apartment in a restored factory in Winstead, and I furnished it for her and I kept my eye on her. And she met a guy who lived on the same floor. He was an alcoholic. She married him.

And he seemed to be sort of okay until it became perfectly clear he was an alcoholic. But he had a burden with her that he didn’t want to handle. He was trying. We were keeping her medications locked up, because at that point she was on...

OWEN: Oxycodone.

VITA: Yes. So she was addicted to oxycodone. And she was drug-seeking everywhere. And what did she say about the pain? She said that the pain was unsupportable, that it was not manageable without the medication. I took her to my doctor. And he knew immediately she was just drug-seeking and was not going to take this in any reasonable way. But she did have real pain.

So when she couldn’t get oxycodone anymore in Winstead, she was able to find heroin.

OWEN: …

VITA: And I didn’t know that she was using heroin.

OWEN: I remember the time I came home and found she had taken my clonazepam. She left three pills, like I wouldn’t notice sixty were gone.

OWEN: And how many times did you and I have family holidays spent in hospital wards because of her?

VITA: Four. Yale, Charlotte Hungerford. It was a reliable way to spend a Thanksgiving. Checked herself out. And there was nothing we could do about it.

I get a phone call at two o’clock in the morning from her husband, who tells me she’s lying on the bathroom floor and she’s not breathing. He said that he came home, and she would cook for him all the time, make him these beautiful meals. He’d come home from work as a superintendent in a school. And so that night, he said he found her on the floor in the bathroom, and he covered her up, and he went and ate his meal. And he didn’t go back till way later. And that shallow breathing turned into no breathing. And by the time he called me, I said, did you call 911? He didn’t call 911. He didn’t have Narcan. None of that.

Because he was tired of it. He didn’t want to be her keeper. She was maddening. He wanted to nurse his own addiction. And she died. And when I called him the next morning, I said, how are you doing? And he said, well, it’s very quiet around here now.

So she got some psychiatric care. She saw Mike Dulchin for one consult, my psychiatrist. And he said she was borderline borderline. She barely met diagnostic criteria for borderline personality disorder.

OWEN: Yeah. But she was rejection sensitive. He wasn’t wrong about that.

VITA: Right. And I remember she gained tremendous weight when she was given olanzapine. And then she got skinny as anything, and I should have known there was something wrong then. She showed up at Grandma’s funeral and she was the size of my pinky finger.

OWEN: What did she say about Dad’s death?

VITA: She came to the service. She came to see him, and she came to the service, and she told the story of how her father, Dad, it was always Dad, who was there, not her biological mother. She went to pottery class. He would take her. She would make an ashtray for Dad. When she had an event at school, it was always Dad. He was really dedicated to his daughter.

OWEN: She said, I feel like I blew my chance with you. And I said, well, you get infinite chances. Forgiveness for family. That’s how this works. Those were my last words.

VITA: When she went to La Varenne, she was twenty, and I told her this story. And she came back to me and said, I would like to be adopted before I fly to Paris. Can we do that? So we did.

OWEN: What does the process of adoption look like for a twenty-year-old?

VITA: Same as anybody else. You go to a lawyer, you tell them what you want to do. He does the paperwork, and that’s that. Any adult can choose to be adopted by anybody. You didn’t have to deal with their biological mother.

She was very happy to be adopted. Born Art Muir’s daughter...

OWEN: ...died your daughter.

VITA: She died two weeks after he did. And the only thing I could think was, thank God he didn’t live to see it.

OWEN: We buried them both in the same hole in the same day.

OWEN: What did you learn from Alison’s life, and her death?

VITA: Never waste perfectly good shrimp shells is a great metaphor for a life. The waste of it. Because she was so rejected as a child. And when a mother rejects a child, I think that’s the worst of all. And it’s almost, at least in my experience, very difficult, if not impossible, to undo that damage. Before you’re adopted, you’re abandoned. You can adopt a child, but you can’t un-abandon them.

OWEN: I can’t un-abandon them.

VITA: Which is really the ceremony she needed.

OWEN: Like an exorcism. We should develop an un-abandonment ritual.

VITA: That could work.

OWEN: And she went to La Varenne to become the first woman to become a chef de cuisine.

VITA: Not to do that, but that was the endgame. It was a long road to that. La Varenne is a fancy cooking school. It was where the wives of rich men went to learn how to cook as a hobby. But it was a serious cooking school. She really learned it, it was very authentic French cooking, from the ground up.

OWEN: It had nothing to do with the Frenchness. It had everything to do with the food. France has a couple of institutions. I think of the Sorbonne.

VITA: As what? That’s a university.

OWEN: Well, sure, but they have the institution for the thing. They are not like the U.S. with the embarrassment of riches around higher education. They’ve got one and you go to the one.

VITA: And French cooking is the cooking for the world, right? That’s the most developed cuisine.

OWEN: I think so too. There isn’t a lot of room for improvisation. In standard, dyed-in-the-wool French cuisine, they’re a rule.

VITA: Well, it’s a textual religion. It’s pretty obsessive. She would say things like, I can’t follow rules. I read cookbooks for ideas and then I go cook. Julia Child told you that you put the thing in the middle third of the oven and you cooked it for seven and a half minutes.

OWEN: This wasn’t a peasant cuisine.

VITA: No, this is for the high class.

OWEN: And when she came back and started her working life, what was that like?

VITA: Well, I sat her down. I can remember sitting at your father’s desk up in the Eyrie. Where can you take this? You could work in a restaurant. You could teach. She said, well, how would I do that? And so I said, maybe you could intern somewhere, and see if you could get some sort of credential from doing that. And there was a school that had started in Farmington, which wasn’t far from us. So she went there to work.

Then having had that background, she went to work in various restaurants in the area. And there was always one disaster after another, because restaurants are full of people who are overworked, underpaid, and exhausted. So there’s a high incidence of substance abuse in restaurants. She worked in a chic little bistro in New Milford. But the owner was a dreadful alcoholic, and by the time the evening was over, he was really in his cups, so she got stuck doing everything. And he had this industrial-sized box of Saran Wrap. So she’s cleaning up things and wrapping things, and it’s not in a holder, which it should have been. She pulls it down accidentally on herself, and that blade cut her wrist so that she had to have immediate restorative surgery for this dreadful injury.

And she also had a congenital malformation of the end of her back. Coincidentally, I have the same thing. It’s called spondylolisthesis, and it’s not contagious. We were both born with it. And you don’t want to overstress that sacral area. And she was doing it all the time, because they would send her, the sous chef, or the assistant to the sous chef, down to the basement to bring up a bushel of potatoes.

She ended up at the French Culinary Institute in Manhattan.

I have a picture of her in her chef’s attire. She looks suntanned in that picture. And her hair is drawn back, because you’ve got to have your hair out of the way. She clipped it back with an elastic. She had a wonderful head of really curly, unruly hair that now people love, but then she was always trying to straighten. And the chef’s uniform is wonderful. It was a sort of Mandarin collar that you buttoned to the side, and then she had an apron that came around and tied in the front. Pure white. All pure white. She had trouble with her feet, so she wore those clogs.

They had a restaurant they called L’Ecole, where their students would train and work, and it served the public.

OWEN: Training ground.

VITA: I had vichyssoise, the potato leek soup. It was the first time I ever had a chilled soup, and I’ve loved chilled soup to this day. So she taught the students there, and they loved her, because she was very authentic and very funny and very dedicated. At the end of every school session they would give her presents, like a Cuisinart. And I’ll never forget her doing a class there. She’s facing the audience, and she’s got a little cooking station, and she’s making something with shrimp, and she’s showing you that you use the shells of the shrimp. You don’t waste anything. You boil that up and you get an essence of shrimp. She said, “Remember, never waste perfectly good shrimp shells.”

So she did all right there, but I think she had started using something when she was there.

OWEN: It would make sense that she was exposed to enough substances.

VITA: And she started to become paranoid. So-and-so was taking her food out of the refrigerator, or putting stuff in the refrigerator that would get her in trouble.

OWEN: Some of this is true, because I’ve heard these stories from other people. There is backstabbing in the kitchen.

VITA: Right. Highly patriarchal. So she decided she would get out of that and go to something else. She had gotten divorced from this first husband already.

OWEN: Useless man.

VITA: So she looked for another job, and she saw a job for a person who lived in Columbus, Ohio. And it turned out to be the person. There’s only one person who matters who lives in Columbus, Ohio. Leslie Wexner. And we didn’t know anything about Leslie Wexner at the time. It turned out that he owned Victoria’s Secret. And she was hired to be the chef for the family and all the visitors who would come in their airplanes.

OWEN: Jeffrey Epstein.

VITA: Yes. Like, literally, she was cooking for Jeffrey. She said that this man’s estate had twenty-seven kitchens. And she’s expected to cook for everybody. The guests would come, and they would come with the wife and the kids, and the nannies for the kids, and she was expected to cook for everybody. And she didn’t even have help in the kitchen or anyone to clean up. And finally, her back really gave out, and his physician said, " That girl has to go to bed, and she’s got to stay there for nine weeks.” They had her up in, I don’t know, a week.

So she applied for a job at the Culinary Institute of America.

OWEN: And she did get it.

VITA: She did get it. And the job was Chef de Cuisine. So your sister Lindsay went to Columbus and stayed with her, helping her through the recovery period after the surgery.

So she goes to a doctor, she finds a Doctor Feelgood, who slaps morphine patches on her arms. She figured out how to accelerate the delivery of morphine. You put a hairdryer on it, and you make it come faster, or you put two of them on, and it’s even better.

OWEN: These were fentanyl patches.

VITA: Yes. And none of us knew what fentanyl was.

OWEN: What year was this?

VITA: We lived in Washington, Connecticut at the time.

OWEN: 1987. Well, before the opioid epidemic was a thing, anyone knew about. These were still drugs that treated pain.

VITA: So she disappeared off the face of the planet at one point, and your father and I went to find her, to see her apartment in disarray. We finally found her and took her to a hospital. The hospital said no, we don’t treat this sort of thing. Then we went through three hospitals in one night. The last one said, well, this has been legally prescribed to her. She’s an adult. This hospital doesn’t want to have anything to do with it. So they won’t admit her.

And you and I know from experience now that had they admitted her, it would have been a seventy-two hour hold anyway. So your father and I put her in the car. We figured we’d take her home, because nobody had eaten all day. She’s in the back, and she starts talking to us. She says, what did you guys do all day?

And the next day she was literally out of her mind. She was searching madly on the floor in her room, in her purse. She was looking for drugs that might have fallen in the bottom of the purse. So I called the doctor she had been seeing in Tivoli. And he said, you want to be very careful. She could be dangerous. And get her to a hospital as soon as you can.

OWEN: Which you had done the day before.

VITA: So I took her to the hospital. Your father was probably gone, because he was gone five or six days a week. So this was all me. All me, all the time.

OWEN: With your adopted child.

VITA: Yes. And so I take her to the hospital, and we leave her there. But they don’t put her in the psychiatric ward. They put her in the medical ward. I go the next morning and I walk into the bathroom, and there’s no sink in the bathroom. And I go to the nursing station and I said, are you aware of the fact that there’s no sink in that bathroom? They said yes. I said, and? They said she ripped it out of the wall.

Then they put her in the psychiatric ward. And they were so bad, and she was so manipulative, that she got them to give her, I forget what drug it was...

OWEN: Vicodin.

VITA: Yeah, one of those drugs. Completely contraindicated. Twenty years of her leading this failed life, me trying to save what was left of it.

Her first suicide attempt, was that when she slashed her wrist?

OWEN: No, there was a throat one. Was that not the first?

VITA: There was a wrist, but there was a throat. I remember the scar very clearly. There were some attempts I’m blocking out.

OWEN: She was evaluated in an ER for slashing her throat. She then, a week later, was admitted after the acetaminophen overdose that led to liver toxicity.

VITA: Right. And so on that one, she was then living in New Jersey, because I think she got a job there, a teaching job. So I go to the hospital, and they tell me that she’s got liver failure.

OWEN: I believe what you told me on the phone was, “We don’t waste good livers on suicides.”

VITA: So that’s what they said. And miraculously she recovered. And from that day on, she was mine. I brought her home to live with us. I took her to meetings at the hospital. We tried to support her and get her an apartment, to see if she could manage on her own. And this went on and on and on and on.

And it was hopeless. It was absolutely hopeless. She got a job in Philadelphia, and she was involved in some sort of fire. We never got the details of this. She said something caught on fire on the stove.

OWEN: I heard the report from the doctor. There was a shoe on the stove.

VITA: She left her shoe on the stove. But at the same time, there was an injury to her leg that she said came from someone who broke into the apartment. She might have been conflating two stories.

So she was in the hospital for some time, and then they sent her to a nursing home to recover further from this ghastly leg wound.

OWEN: I remember. That was when I was in residency. I talked to the doctor briefly, and he said she had a mini-mental status exam score of thirteen, which is in the demented range. I guess it was delirium at the time, but they didn’t seem to understand that.

VITA: Anyway, so then we rescued her from that. I couldn’t make the trip. So dear Albert Rivera did it for me. He went and picked her up with all her stuff and brought her home. And so she was living at home, driving your father, who was ill, absolutely nuts, because she had logorrhea. He’d sit down and try to relax and watch a program on television, and she wouldn’t stop talking. And this was after his first stroke in France. That was a left MCA stroke, so his receptive language was impaired. And I’m dealing with both of them simultaneously, and a full-time challenging job. That was a circus.

She got on Social Security disability, which she really needed to be on. She was legitimately disabled. And I found her an apartment. It was the worst decision of my life. I found an apartment in a restored factory in Winstead, and I furnished it for her and I kept my eye on her. And she met a guy who lived on the same floor. He was an alcoholic. She married him.

And he seemed to be sort of okay until it became perfectly clear he was an alcoholic. But he had a burden with her that he didn’t want to handle. He was trying. We were keeping her medications locked up, because at that point she was on...

OWEN: Oxycodone.

VITA: Yes. So she was addicted to oxycodone. And she was drug-seeking everywhere. And what did she say about the pain? She said that the pain was unsupportable, that it was not manageable without the medication. I took her to my doctor. And he knew immediately she was just drug-seeking and was not going to take this in any reasonable way. But she did have real pain.

So when she couldn’t get oxycodone anymore in Winstead, she was able to find heroin.

OWEN: …

VITA: And I didn’t know that she was using heroin.

OWEN: I remember the time I came home and found she had taken my clonazepam. She left three pills, like I wouldn’t notice sixty were gone.

OWEN: And how many times did you and I have family holidays spent in hospital wards because of her?

VITA: Four. Yale, Charlotte Hungerford. It was a reliable way to spend a Thanksgiving. Checked herself out. And there was nothing we could do about it.

I get a phone call at two o’clock in the morning from her husband, who tells me she’s lying on the bathroom floor and she’s not breathing. He said that he came home, and she would cook for him all the time, make him these beautiful meals. He’d come home from work as a superintendent in a school. And so that night, he said he found her on the floor in the bathroom, and he covered her up, and he went and ate his meal. And he didn’t go back till way later. And that shallow breathing turned into no breathing. And by the time he called me, I said, did you call 911? He didn’t call 911. He didn’t have Narcan. None of that.

Because he was tired of it. He didn’t want to be her keeper. She was maddening. He wanted to nurse his own addiction. And she died. And when I called him the next morning, I said, how are you doing? And he said, well, it’s very quiet around here now.

So she got some psychiatric care. She saw Mike Dulchin for one consult, my psychiatrist. And he said she was borderline borderline. She barely met diagnostic criteria for borderline personality disorder.

OWEN: Yeah. But she was rejection sensitive. He wasn’t wrong about that.

VITA: Right. And I remember she gained tremendous weight when she was given olanzapine. And then she got skinny as anything, and I should have known there was something wrong then. She showed up at Grandma’s funeral and she was the size of my pinky finger.

OWEN: What did she say about Dad’s death?

VITA: She came to the service. She came to see him, and she came to the service, and she told the story of how her father, Dad, it was always Dad, who was there, not her biological mother. She went to pottery class. He would take her. She would make an ashtray for Dad. When she had an event at school, it was always Dad. He was really dedicated to his daughter.

OWEN : She said, I feel like I blew my chance with you. And I said, well, you get infinite chances. Forgiveness for family. That’s how this works. Those were my last words.

VITA : When she went to La Varenne, she was twenty, and I told her this story. And she came back to me and said, I would like to be adopted before I fly to Paris. Can we do that? So we did.

OWEN: What does the process of adoption look like for a twenty-year-old?

VITA: Same as anybody else. You go to a lawyer, you tell them what you want to do. He does the paperwork, and that’s that. Any adult can choose to be adopted by anybody. You didn’t have to deal with their biological mother.

She was very happy to be adopted. Born Art Muir’s daughter...

OWEN: ...died your daughter.

VITA: She died two weeks after he did. And the only thing I could think was, thank God he didn’t live to see it.

OWEN: We buried them both in the same hole in the same day.

OWEN: What did you learn from Alison’s life, and her death?

VITA: Never waste perfectly good shrimp shells is a great metaphor for a life. The waste of it. Because she was so rejected as a child. And when a mother rejects a child, I think that’s the worst of all. And it’s almost, at least in my experience, very difficult, if not impossible, to undo that damage. Before you’re adopted, you’re abandoned. You can adopt a child, but you can’t un-abandon them.

OWEN: I can’t un-abandon them.

VITA: Which is really the ceremony she needed.

OWEN: Like an exorcism. We should develop an un-abandonment ritual.

VITA: That could work.
